messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi's Vigilance

Kofi Mensah had run Riverside Middle School for twenty-three years with the kind of steady authority that came from believing deeply in order, fairness, and the capacity of young people to flourish when given clear boundaries and genuine care. He was known for walking the hallways at irregular intervals, greeting students by name, noticing when something was wrong. At seventy-seven, he had planned to retire within two years. Then, on a Tuesday evening in March, two former students—both in their mid-twenties, both carrying rage that had calcified over years of perceived slights—cornered him in the parking lot as he locked up his office.

The assault lasted perhaps four minutes. What Kofi remembered with perfect, unbearable clarity was the smell: the sharp fermentation of cheap whiskey on one attacker's breath, mixed with the metallic tang of his own blood. He remembered the moment he realized his body would not obey his commands—that the man holding his arm was stronger, younger, and utterly indifferent to his pleas. He remembered the sound of his own voice breaking as he asked them to stop, the sound of their laughter, the sound of his briefcase hitting the pavement. He remembered the precise instant he understood that no one was coming to help him, that his authority meant nothing here, that he was simply a body to be used.

The police found him twenty minutes later. Three ribs cracked. A concussion. Lacerations that required eighteen stitches. The physical injuries healed within weeks. The other injuries did not.

By the following September, Kofi had developed a rigid ritual around entering any space. The moment he stepped through a doorway—his office, the faculty lounge, the auditorium during assembly—his eyes moved immediately to the exits. Where was the door? Could he reach it quickly? Were there obstacles? His assistant principal, Marcus, had begun to notice that Kofi no longer sat with his back to an open room. At faculty meetings, he positioned himself near the entrance. During student presentations, he stood rather than sat. When a student dropped a textbook behind him, Kofi flinched so violently that his hand went to his chest, his breathing shallow and rapid for several minutes afterward.

What troubled Kofi most deeply was not the physical hypervigilance but the collapse of his sense of himself as capable and trustworthy. He had always been the one others relied upon—parents called seeking his counsel, teachers consulted him on difficult situations, students knew he would listen and act fairly. Now, when his wife Ama suggested they attend their grandson's school play, Kofi heard himself say no, that he was too tired, though he was not tired. The truth was that sitting in a darkened auditorium with strangers on all sides, with exits obscured by rows of seats, filled him with a dread so acute it felt like drowning. He could not trust himself to remain composed. What if he panicked? What if he embarrassed himself, embarrassed Ama? It was easier to stay home.

He had begun to blame himself for the assault itself. If he had not stayed late that evening, if he had taken a different route to his car, if he had been more aware of the two young men lingering near the gymnasium—if he had simply been more careful, more vigilant, more something—it would not have happened. Yet simultaneously, he had come to believe that no amount of vigilance would ever be enough. He could not rely on his own judgment to keep himself safe. He could not rely on the police, who had found the attackers but who seemed uninterested in pressing charges. He could not even rely on Ama, who loved him but who could not understand why he would not simply "move past it" and return to normal.

By November, Kofi had taken medical leave. The school board was sympathetic; he was a respected administrator with decades of service. But Kofi understood the truth: he was afraid of his own students, afraid of the parking lot, afraid of the moment when his vigilance might fail and something terrible would happen again. When he remembered the assault, he sometimes heard nothing but the laughter—it played in his mind like a recording he could not stop. Other times, he recalled the details with such vivid precision that his body responded as if it were happening again, his heart racing, his palms sweating. And then there were the moments when he could think about it clinically, as though describing something that had happened to someone else, and feel nothing at all—a numbness so complete it frightened him more than the grief did.

Ama finally insisted he see someone. She said it quietly, with the firmness that had sustained their marriage for fifty-two years: "You are disappearing, and I cannot watch this alone." Kofi made an appointment with Dr. Hassan, a therapist his primary care physician had recommended. He sat in the waiting room, scanning for exits, his leg bouncing, uncertain whether he had made a terrible mistake or finally taken the only step that might matter.
